The 12th Annual Drug Policy Foundation Conference
– A Headless Movement or Horizontal Organization?
Analysis By Richard Cowan

The broader drug reform movement is adrift. The Drug Policy Foundation is being run by its excellent staff, but there is no "executive director" again -- or still.

The staff did a good job of putting on the conference, but there is a reason that organizations – and movements -- have leaders. There was once a time -- when Arnold Trebach was there – that the DPF served that purpose.

Nonetheless, there is much progress being made as the various groups go their own way. This lack of "leadership" may prove to be a healthy development.

In addition, the buzz of the conference was the news that the Lindesmith Center is moving out from under the Soros umbrella. This may mean that Soros’ Open Society Institute will be more direct, but less visible, in funding anti-prohibitionist causes. Or it may just mean that Soros will do less funding.

Soros himself has observed that some of his philanthropies have counterproductive. That has sometimes been the case with the funding of some parts of the so-called harm-reduction movement. The irony of this is that Soros is a prohibitionist, who is vilified for supporting "the legalization of all drugs."

One of the highlights of the conference for me was hearing Keith Stroup, the founder and Natiional Director of NORML declare again that NORML is in favor of the legalization of marijuana. It does not run from the "L-word," and seeks to represent the interests of the millions of DEAland marijuana smokers.

This has been NORML’s position from its inception, and it does not hide behind the "harm-reduction" label – unlike others, who use it to appear to be something that they are not.

There is no conflict between the objectives of reducing the dangers of hard drug use and legalizing marijuana, but they really are two different subjects. However, any realistic effort to reduce hard drug use must begin with the legalization of marijuana, not with subsuming marijuana reform under the harm-reduction rubric.

See
"Those who insist on keeping the plant illegal bear a serious degree of moral responsibility for young marijuana users who do go on to use cocaine, heroin, PCP or other genuinely dangerous or addictive drugs."
Alan Bock, of the Orange County Register On the Real Gateway
and
What If Marijuana Disappeared? By Richard Cowan
and links

Thus, a clear stand in favor of the legalization of marijuana is the best way to advance "harm-reduction."

I always find attending conferences involves a trade-off between watching panels from which I often learn a lot, and meeting old friends, from whom I often learn even more. This year I chose the latter course and missed most of the sessions.

Naturally, one of the sessions that I attended one on the Internet that featured Mark Greer of Mapinc.org and Adam Smith of DRCnet.org. It was moderated by Barbara Bode, a very impressive Washington based consultant.

The consensus was that we are winning on the Net, but that we cannot rest on our laurels.

Separately, I met with Adam Smith and Kris Lotlikar to talk about their efforts in organizing the campuses to repeal the ban on loans for students convicted of even minor marijuana offenses – but not violent crimes. I think that this could the spark that will awaken the campuses. Adam is an exceptionally bright young man, and the ideal person to lead this effort.
See
Chicago Tribune Reports Campus Opposition Growing
To Higher Education Act’s Ban On Loans To Students Convicted Of "Drug" Possession.

Conversations with Canadians provided another high point.

First, I got to meet Matt Elrod, the amazing webmaster of Mapinc.org. He has been very helpful to me since they began hosting MarijuanaNews. Mapinc is one of the institutions that is thriving in a polycentric anti-prohibitionist movement. Of course, it would thrive even more with more support.

I also enjoyed a long conversation with Eugene Oscapella of the Canadian Foundation for Drug Policy, who is one of the most knowledgeable observers of the scene. Nonetheless, he is as puzzled as everyone else by the slowness of the Canadian government in moving on marijuana reform.

There are only two possible explanations. Either the Prime Minister is totally out of touch with reality, and he is using party discipline to contain things, or there is tremendous behind-the-scenes pressure from DEAland.

These possible reasons are not mutually exclusive, but the lid cannot be kept on much longer. If it is DEAland pressure, then word will get out, with a possibly explosive backlash.

Eugene introduced me to Vancouver Constable Gil Puder.
See
Prohibitionist Calgary Sun Does Friendly Story About Anti-Prohibitionist Vancouver Constable
I have long been a fan of his, and I certainly was not disappointed. He is a very impressive man, whose has shown courage in speaking out against the party line in Canada.


Conferences are both educational and political/social events. I have been to so many of them that the agenda tends to be overshadowed by the people. However, I think that the quality of the people in the anti-prohibitionist movement is the ultimate reason that we will win.

We won the arguments decades ago.

Now we have more and more people who are speaking out, and we have the Internet to coordinate and magnify these efforts. The Net makes decentralized movements more effective. We may be entering an era of horizontal organization. That may be the real theme of the headless DPF conference. 


In the next few days, I will be writing more about what I learned at the conference.
